before: Intentional, meaning you pick one of those acts and decide when you'll do it, and what the smallest first step is (like with the envelope). Some of them are only one step anyway. If it needs money or somebody's help, sort that out before the day, and if you'll have to tell someone something they won't like, say it out loud to yourself ahead of time. At first it'll probably come out sounding like a question.
after: (The next section, "Love Doesn't Have to Wait for Trust", begins: Sometimes love is available and still feels unsafe because love and trust have become tied together as though one has to validate the other. They don’t.… It isn't humanized yet.)
brief:
- Second half of guide paragraph 4: after the day, look at what actually happened. Didn't do it -> don't assume why; it could be fear, not being sure what you were going for, not knowing how, being worn out, something practical. Did it and didn't feel better right away -> it didn't fail. Whether it helped -> the article's own earlier question, "What is this practice supposed to help, and how would I know if it's helping?" (from "When Healing Turns Into Checking"): safer, closer to your little one, more capable, more enjoyable, not just checked off. A short callback to that question can carry this part; it doesn't need explaining again.
Note: the paragraph before is about planning one act (when, the smallest first step, what it needs, saying it out loud to yourself first, which at first "will probably come out sounding like a question").
What failed, all read as AI: every draft walked the guide's order in a parallel "If you didn't do it… / If you did it…" frame, packed the reasons into one "or… or… or" sentence, and ended on a list of what the act adds. One was: "If the day came and went and you didn't do it, maybe you were scared, or not sure what you were going for, or didn't know how, or were too tired, or something practical got in the way. Look at what actually happened before you decide which one it was. Fear can feel a lot like being tired. And if you did do it and didn't feel better right away, you haven't failed, but checking it off doesn't prove it helped either. Keep or adjust it by what it actually added: are you any safer, closer to your little one, more capable, or enjoying things more?"
The author's own lists that pass give each item its own sentence or question with a different start, oddest last, or react to an item. Measure the act by what actually changed, not by how it felt (feeling better right away isn't the test).
The section's first paragraph says the underlying reason people stay in unsafe relationships is a lack of self-love, which the author holds is under all the other reasons (see his ruling). Keep this paragraph consistent with that; don't bring self-love up again.
Your first sentence will be read together with the last lines of the paragraph before.
Limits: don't invent facts about the author's life; never call the inner child "the kid"; don't reuse the article's examples (the envelope, the boundary, the clean room, the keys, sarcasm, the old food, the angry text).
length: three to five sentences, 50 to 100 words
guide_passage: Afterward, review what actually happened. Not doing it may reflect fear, uncertainty about the goal, lack of skill, exhaustion, or a practical barrier; don’t decide which without looking. Completing it without immediate relief is not automatically failure, and completion alone does not prove it helped. Adjust the action to what it actually contributes to safety, connection, competence, or enjoyment—not just to whether it earns a tick.
